title: Natalie Dormer in Anna Karenina - review
transcript: Hello and welcome to theater reviews with Paul 7. I'm here at Chichester Festival Theater to see Natalie Dorma in Anna Corenina. [Music] For the second time in less than a week, I've sat through a play more than 3 hours long. Uh Stereophonic, which I saw a few days ago, was for me too long. But Anna Cora epic though it was was actually too short. It barely gave Toltoy or Natalie Dorma the chance to show off their brilliance. Keep watching and I'll tell you why I thought it was a good try that fell short of doing justice to a great novel. But first, please like, comment, and subscribe to this channel. Hello, I'm Paul 7 Lewis and in these reviews I tried to tell you what the show is about, describe the production and report back on how the actors get on with it. At 3 hours, this stage adaptation of Anna Corenina by Philip Breen can only hope to present a fraction of Toltoy's novel, which runs to 38 hours on audible. Now, Mr. Sabrina has chosen to try to tell the stories of all three of the main women, Anna, Dolly, and Kitty. As a result, none of them get a full swing at their characters in the time available. Nevertheless, the actors give impressive performances, not least Natalie Dorma as Anna, who within the scope she's given brings a tornado of emotion to the role. So much so that you find yourself longing for her next moment on stage. She's got a rich Colorado voice that is like a fullbodied red wine. Her piercing eyes and curling mouth give passion to her words. Naomi Sheldon as Dolly is wonderfully over the top as she harangs her useless philandering husband and bemons her aging body and rails against everything with a terade of very modern exploitives. Incidentally, I thought the use of contemporary uh language, particularly sexual terms, while anacronistic, did work well as shorthand for the character's feelings. Kitty was the most one-dimensional of the main protagonist, but Shalishia James Davis made the most of what she was given, which was a woman constantly on the verge of a nav breakdown as she assesses her obsessive suitor then husband. The actors certainly convey the essence of their characters, but inevitably much color is lost. A great deal of narrative is also lost to what much of the time becomes more like a plot summary. So what is the plot? Well, Anna's dissatisfied with ordinary family life and with her husband Karen, a seemingly nice, tolerant chap and nicely played by Tamua Edun. She leaves him for a more passionate life with her lover Veronsky, whose firecracker character is well conveyed by Sheamus Delain. However, this being mid-9th century Russia, she finds herself ostracized from society and separated from her children. Worse still, she begins to doubt Fronk's faithfulness. In fact, all the men seem to have a roving eye whether they act upon it or not. Two other unhappy relationships are explored. Leaven, played with passion by David Oats, loves Kitty, but she resists him. She thinks he'll be unfaithful because of his past record of bed hopping. Eventually, she's reassured and marries him, but her doubts continue right up to a traumatic childbirth. Dolly's already well into a marriage and has many, too many children. Her husband Stever gamles and womanizes in a splendidly spineless characterization by Johnny Broadbent and she constantly rails at him and at her own perceived lack of attractiveness. The problem with this filiting approach is that we you lose much of the complexity of characters and their lives. Rather than the flesh, what we get are the bare bones of the plot. And when it comes down to it, plot is only the structure on which good novels and plays build their characters development. Instead, this adaptation really reduces these three women to people who don't trust their partners, shout and cry a lot, and end more or less happier than they began. And Tolstein's novel is a great deal more than that. The other challenge is how to design it. The open chichester stage doesn't allow for solid scenery except at the very back. So how to present horses and trains very important components of this story. Now since the adapter Philip Breen is also the director we can assume he had a hand in the approach. Now although Matt Jones design is very busy with many chairs that are moved around the most noticeable aspect is a nursery theme. Children's toys are scattered around the stage. dolls houses, horses, a train set. It serves to emphasize perhaps that women in this period are still treated like children in terms of their rights. I'm pretty sure the doll's houses were meant to remind us of Ipsson's play about another woman trapped in domesticity. A part which Natalie Dorma surely must play at some point. The train set reminds us that the world is changing. Modern inventions such as the railways and electricity have arrived. And while the former is central to the story, the latter is also given its moment in the spotlight, so to speak, in the form of tubes of light which descend and form, of course, a cage. The wooden horses come in handy as substitutes for the real thing, but frankly, the sight of a man shooting an injured rocking horse was comical. shades of Montipython and Spamalot. And when Les Dennis, in a delightful cameo as the worldweary servant pet cat, drives a carriage drawn by a wooden horse. It's silly rather than amusing. I would rather have used my imagination more. Uh, something which we had to do when it came to the allimportant trade. I did like many of the effects. The trio of Japanese musicians who played Paddikanine's edgy music. The way the large cast and there are 19 named actors sat in chairs at the back of the stage um es especially at the moment when they scraped cutlery together during a dining scene. There are too many short scenes which become messy. But there are some scenes which really hit home like Anna's secretive visit to see her son. A rare moment when you really understand profoundly what she's given up. This adaptation of Toltoy's novel is a brave attempt, but like Scott's Trek to the South Pole, it falls short of total success. I give Anna Karenina three stars.
